```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(readr)
library(arrow)
library(jsonlite)

d1_figures <- here("output", "deliverable1", "figures")
d2_figures <- here("output", "deliverable2", "figures")
d3_figures <- here("output", "deliverable3", "figures")
d4_figures <- here("output", "deliverable4", "figures")
d5_figures <- here("output", "deliverable5", "figures")

d1_technology <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable1", "tables", "table1_by_technology.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
d1_coverage <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable1", "tables", "table_meeting_coverage.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
d2_snapshot <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable2", "tables", "02_snapshot.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
d2_duration <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable2", "tables", "02_duration_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
d3_energy <- read_parquet(here("data", "analysis", "projects_combined.parquet"),
                          col_select = c("project_energy_type", "process_type")) %>%
  group_by(project_energy_type, process_type) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = process_type, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(Total = rowSums(select(., -project_energy_type), na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  rename(
    `Energy Type` = project_energy_type,
    `Categorical Exclusion` = CE,
    `Environmental Assessment` = EA,
    `Environmental Impact Statement` = EIS
  )
d4_hubs <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable4", "tables", "table_department_collaboration_hubs.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
d5_compliance <- read_csv(here("output", "deliverable5", "tables", "05_fra_compliance.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

clean_row <- d3_energy %>% filter(`Energy Type` == "Clean")
fossil_row <- d3_energy %>% filter(`Energy Type` == "Fossil")
other_row <- d3_energy %>% filter(`Energy Type` == "Other")

clean_total <- clean_row$Total[[1]]
clean_ce_pct <- clean_row$`Categorical Exclusion`[[1]] / clean_total
fossil_ce_pct <- fossil_row$`Categorical Exclusion`[[1]] / fossil_row$Total[[1]]
other_ce_pct <- other_row$`Categorical Exclusion`[[1]] / other_row$Total[[1]]

solar_row <- d1_technology %>% filter(Technology == "Renewable Energy Production - Solar")
solar_total <- solar_row$Total[[1]]
solar_ce_pct <- solar_row$`Categorical Exclusion`[[1]] / solar_total
solar_eis_pct <- solar_row$`Environmental Impact Statement`[[1]] / solar_total
solar_ea_pct <- solar_row$`Environmental Assessment`[[1]] / solar_total

doe_row <- d1_coverage %>% filter(lead_agency_harmonized == "Department of Energy")
doe_total <- doe_row$Total[[1]]
doe_ce_pct <- doe_row$CE[[1]] / doe_total

n_reviews <- d2_snapshot %>% filter(process_type == "All") %>% pull(row_total) %>% first()
n_programmatic <- d2_snapshot %>% filter(process_type == "All", review_type == "Programmatic") %>% pull(n)
n_tiered <- d2_snapshot %>% filter(process_type == "All", review_type == "Tiered") %>% pull(n)
n_nonstandard <- n_programmatic + n_tiered
pct_nonstandard <- n_nonstandard / n_reviews

ea_standard_med <- d2_duration %>% filter(process_type == "EA", review_type == "Standard") %>% pull(median_days)
ea_tiered_med <- d2_duration %>% filter(process_type == "EA", review_type == "Tiered") %>% pull(median_days)
eis_standard_med <- d2_duration %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", review_type == "Standard") %>% pull(median_days)
eis_programmatic_med <- d2_duration %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", review_type == "Programmatic") %>% pull(median_days)
eis_tiered_med <- d2_duration %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", review_type == "Tiered") %>% pull(median_days)

doe_bridge <- d4_hubs %>% filter(department == "Department of Energy") %>% pull(`Bridge score`)
doi_bridge <- d4_hubs %>% filter(department == "Department of the Interior") %>% pull(`Bridge score`)

ea_post_fra_total <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EA") %>% pull(total) %>% first()
eis_post_fra_total <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EIS") %>% pull(total) %>% first()
ea_exceeds_pct <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EA", compliance == "Exceeds limit") %>% pull(pct) / 100
ea_compliant_pct <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EA", compliance == "Compliant") %>% pull(pct) / 100
eis_exceeds_standard_pct <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", compliance == "Exceeds standard limit") %>% pull(pct) / 100
eis_exceeds_limit_pct <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", compliance == "Exceeds limit") %>% pull(pct) / 100
eis_compliant_pct <- d5_compliance %>% filter(process_type == "EIS", compliance == "Compliant") %>% pull(pct) / 100
```

## Executive Summary

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Findings

- **There are diminishing returns to broad NEPA reform for decarbonization since they are not likely to require major federal review (EA or EIS).** Most decarbonization projects in this corpus use Categorical Exclusions: `r scales::percent(clean_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` for decarbonization projects overall, versus `r scales::percent(fossil_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` for fossil energy and `r scales::percent(other_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` for other project types. 
- **There are real efficiency gains to be had in agency-level implementation.** Programmatic and tiered reviews remain rare (`r n_nonstandard` of `r scales::comma(n_reviews)` decarbonization EA/EIS reviews; `r scales::percent(pct_nonstandard, accuracy = 0.1)`), but tiered EISs are faster on median than standard and programmatic EISs (`r eis_tiered_med`, `r eis_standard_med`, and `r eis_programmatic_med` days, respectively).
- **Permitting reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 have had a real, but modest, impact.** Post-FRA, `r scales::percent(ea_exceeds_pct, accuracy = 1)` of EAs still exceed the 75-page limit; for EISs, `r scales::percent(eis_exceeds_limit_pct, accuracy = 1)` exceed 300 pages and another `r scales::percent(eis_exceeds_standard_pct, accuracy = 1)` fall between 151 and 300 pages.
:::

# 1. There Are Diminishing Returns to NEPA Reform for Speeding Decarbonization Projects

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.column-margin .review-comment}
How are these as alternative, catchier options for this first point?

<br>

- **The dirty secret of NEPA reform: it mostly helps the wrong projects:** the vast majority of decarbonization-related projects never require environmental assessment or environmental impact statements

- **Streamlining NEPA won't supercharge the clean energy transition**—the vast majority of decarbonization-related projects never require environmental assessment or environmental impact statements.

:::
:::

### 1.1 Decarbonization projects use categorical exclusions at higher rates than fossil fuel or other project types; fossil fuel projects have higher EA/EIS rates than decarbonization projects.

Across `r scales::comma(clean_total)` decarbonization actions, `r scales::percent(clean_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` use Categorical Exclusions. That is materially higher than the CE share for fossil projects (`r scales::percent(fossil_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)`) and for the residual "other" category (`r scales::percent(other_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)`). That means reforms aimed only at accelerating EAs and EISs will affect only a limited slice of the decarbonization pipeline.

### 1.2 The most comprehensive EA and CE data show that 97% of decarbonization-related actions are categorically excluded.

We have the most complete project coverage for Department of Energy (DOE) and Department of the Interioer (DOI) records, which show the overwhelming majority of actions are Categorically Excluded (CE). For DOE, approximately 97% are processed via CEs; whereas DOI reports a higher rates of EA and EIS but remains heavily CE-weighted. Although DOE or DOI are not necessarily representative of every federal agency, this finding indicates that where the underlying review process coverage is complete, the decarbonization portfolio is overwhelmingly concentrated in the lowest-intensity NEPA pathway.

### 1.3 NEPA is just not really a problem for solar.

Within the current technology-tagged output, there are `r scales::comma(solar_total)` solar actions total; `r scales::percent(solar_ce_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` are CEs, `r scales::percent(solar_ea_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` are EAs, and only `r scales::percent(solar_eis_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` are EISs. Within this federal-review corpus, NEPA is likely not the main bottleneck for most solar activity. Other constraints such as transmission access, interconnection, land availability, agency capacity, and financing may matter more than full-scale NEPA review.

```{r}
#| label: fig-technology-by-process
#| fig-cap: "Decarbonization technology tags by NEPA review process. Solar is heavily CE-driven, while some technologies show higher EA/EIS shares. Non-solar bars are de-emphasized to draw attention to solar's CE dominance."
#| out-width: "95%"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

# --- Solar-highlight variant (key_insights only; original deliverable 1 figure unchanged) ---

# CATF colors (replicated locally; no dependency on 00_setup.R)
.catf_dark_blue <- "#0047BB"
.catf_teal      <- "#00AE8D"
.catf_magenta   <- "#C22A90"
.solar_amber    <- "#D4720A"   # warm amber for the callout border

# Technology tags (identical to deliverable 1 constants)
.clean_tags <- c(
  "Carbon Capture and Sequestration",
  "Conventional Energy Production - Nuclear",
  "Conventional Energy Production - Other",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Biomass",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Energy Storage",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Geothermal",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Hydrokinetic",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Hydropower",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Other",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Solar",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Wind, Offshore",
  "Renewable Energy Production - Wind, Onshore",
  "Nuclear Technology",
  "Electricity Transmission",
  "Utilities (electricity, gas, telecommunications)"
)

# Read only the columns needed
.proj <- read_parquet(
  here("data", "analysis", "projects_combined.parquet"),
  col_select = c("project_title", "project_type", "process_type", "project_energy_type")
)

.ce <- .proj |>
  filter(project_energy_type == "Clean") |>
  mutate(project_type_list = map(project_type, \(x) {
    if (is.na(x) || x == "") return(character(0))
    tryCatch(fromJSON(x), error = \(e) character(0))
  }))

# Row order: ascending percent_projects (bottom-to-top on the y-axis)
.order_df <- .ce |>
  select(project_title, project_type_list) |>
  unnest(project_type_list) |>
  rename(technology = project_type_list) |>
  filter(technology %in% .clean_tags) |>
  distinct(project_title, technology) |>
  count(technology, name = "n") |>
  mutate(
    pct = 100 * n / n_distinct(.ce$project_title),
    technology_label = case_when(
      technology == "Renewable Energy Production - Other" ~ technology,
      TRUE ~ str_remove(technology, "^Renewable Energy Production - ")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(pct)  # ascending -> bottom-to-top factor order

.label_order <- .order_df$technology_label

# Main plotting dataset
.dat <- .ce |>
  select(project_title, project_type_list, process_type) |>
  unnest(project_type_list) |>
  rename(technology = project_type_list) |>
  filter(technology %in% .clean_tags) |>
  distinct(project_title, technology, process_type) |>
  count(technology, process_type, name = "n") |>
  group_by(technology) |>
  mutate(
    share = n / sum(n),
    technology_label = case_when(
      technology == "Renewable Energy Production - Other" ~ technology,
      TRUE ~ str_remove(technology, "^Renewable Energy Production - ")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    technology_label = factor(technology_label, levels = .label_order),
    is_solar = as.character(technology_label == "Solar")  # "TRUE"/"FALSE" for scale_alpha_manual
  )

.totals <- .dat |>
  group_by(technology_label) |>
  summarise(total = sum(n), .groups = "drop")

# Numeric y-position of the Solar bar (factor level index)
.solar_idx <- which(.label_order == "Solar")

# Build the figure
fig_solar_highlight <- ggplot(.dat,
  aes(x = share, y = technology_label, fill = process_type)) +

  # 1. Warm background stripe spanning full panel width behind the solar row
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf,
    ymin = .solar_idx - 0.5, ymax = .solar_idx + 0.5,
    fill = "#FFF3CD", color = NA
  ) +

  # 2. Stacked bars — non-solar dimmed to 20% opacity, solar at full opacity
  geom_col(aes(alpha = is_solar), width = 0.8) +

  # 3. Percentage labels inside bars (full opacity for readability throughout)
  geom_text(
    aes(label = ifelse(share >= 0.03, scales::percent(share, accuracy = 1), "")),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    size = 3,
    color = "white"
  ) +

  # 4. Total project counts to the right of each bar
  geom_text(
    data = .totals,
    aes(x = 1.02, y = technology_label, label = scales::comma(total)),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3,
    color = "gray30"
  ) +

  # 5. Amber border framing the solar bar exactly (drawn on top of bars)
  annotate("rect",
    xmin = 0, xmax = 1,
    ymin = .solar_idx - 0.4, ymax = .solar_idx + 0.4,
    fill = NA, color = .solar_amber, linewidth = 1.5
  ) +

  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("CE" = .catf_dark_blue, "EA" = .catf_teal, "EIS" = .catf_magenta)
  ) +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = 0.45, "TRUE" = 1.0),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Share of Projects",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Process Type",
    title = "Actions with Decarbonization Tag by Technology and Process Type",
    caption = "Note: Percentage labels below 3% are excluded for readability."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# Save standalone PNG for circulation (highlighted variant only; does not overwrite original)
ggsave(
  filename = here(d1_figures, "02_clean_energy_bar_solar_highlight.png"),
  plot = fig_solar_highlight,
  width = 10,
  height = 6,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)

fig_solar_highlight
```

# 2. There Are Real Efficiency Gains to Be Had in NEPA Implementation at the Agency Level

### 2.1 Increased strategic use of programmatic and tiered reviews.

The evidence on programmatic and tiered reviews indicates that there are real efficiency gains from avoiding project-specific environmental impact statements. However, programmatic and tiered reviews are rare: only `r n_nonstandard` of `r scales::comma(n_reviews)` decarbonization EA/EIS reviews (`r scales::percent(pct_nonstandard, accuracy = 0.1)`) are programmatic or tiered, indicating that there are opportunities for agencies to increase their use, as appropriate.

Tiered EAs take longer than standard EAs on average (`r ea_tiered_med` versus `r ea_standard_med` days), but have a substantially shorter timeline than a full EIS. This suggests the real efficiency gain from tiering is when it allows an agency to avoid a full EIS altogether rather than just shortening the timeline of an EA. Tiered EISs take less time than standard and programmatic EISs (though distributions substantially overlap and sample sizes are small)

```{r}
#| label: fig-review-duration
#| fig-cap: "Review duration by review type and NEPA process. Small sample sizes mean the results should be treated as directional, not definitive."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d2_figures, "02_duration.png"))
```

### 2.2 Increased interagency coordination. 

[Previous CATF research](https://www.catf.us/resource/evidence-based-recommendations-overcoming-barriers-federal-transmission-permitting/) on transmission permitting has demonstrated that insufficient support for agency coordination, cooperation, and capacity contributes to longer permitting timelines. This research builds on that finding by mapping which agencies collaborate the most on NEPA reviews. We find that DOE stands out as the clear hub of the multi-department netwxork, with a bridge score of `r round(doe_bridge, 1)` compared with `r round(doi_bridge, 1)` for DOI. That suggests that improving DOE-DOI collaboration through targeted staffing increases, memoranda of understanding, and other mechanisms may have outsized impact on review timelines. Its dominance reflects both the sheer number of partner agencies (9 unique departments) and the high volume of shared project ties. DOI is a meaningful secondary hub, with its strongest partnership running back to DOE. All other departments are more peripheral—connecting to one or two partners and typically anchored to DOE as their primary collaborator. This indicates that improving DOE-DOI collaboration through targeted staffing increases, memoranda of understanding, and other mechanisms may have outsized impact on improving review timelines.

```{r}
#| label: fig-department-sankey
#| fig-cap: "Cross-department project flows. DOE is the dominant node in the multi-department collaboration network."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d4_figures, "fig_department_sankey.png"))
```

# 3. Permitting Reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 Have Had a Real, but Modest, Impact

The [Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (Public Law 118-5)](https://ceq.doe.gov/laws-regulations/fra.html) introduced page limits for NEPA environmental reviews. Under the law, environmental assessments must be 75 pages or less and environmental impact statements must be either 150 pages or less, or for proposals of extraordinary complexity, under 300 pages or less.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.column-margin .review-comment}
I rewrote/restructured some of the content in this section -- tell me what you think. 

:::
:::

There is considerable variation in average page length of documents over time. Using a 3-month rollling average, we see a slight decline in average page length after FRA's passage, but a return to pre-FRA rates more recently. To some extent, this is likely a result of a small sample size post-FRA: only `r ea_post_fra_total` EAs and `r eis_post_fra_total` EISs.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pages-over-time
#| fig-cap: "Regulatory page counts over time, with FRA enactment marked by the vertical red line. Post-FRA lengths decline, but the sample remains limited."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d5_figures, "05_pages_over_time_break.png"))
```

Viewed another way, our analysis shows a real but modest post-FRA shift in document length pre- and post-FRA. Average and median regulatory page counts mostly decline after the FRA threshold, which is consistent with agencies responding to the new statutory limits. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-pre-post
#| fig-cap: "Mean regulatory pages for decarbonization EA and EIS projects, before and after FRA enactment."
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d5_figures, "05_pages_pre_post_fra.png"))
```

Ultimately, it's like that instituting page limits had some effect, but the evidence is not yet definitive:`r scales::percent(ea_compliant_pct, accuracy = 1)` of post-FRA EAs are compliant with the 75-page limit; and  `r scales::percent(eis_exceeds_standard_pct, accuracy = 1)` ofEISs fall within the 151--300 page limit, with another `r scales::percent(eis_compliant_pct, accuracy = 1)` potentially being compliant under the "extraordinary complexity" exception for under 300 pages.  The practical conclusion is that the FRA has changed incentives, but not yet produced consistent compliance. A fuller assessment will require more decisions from EA and EIS projects initiated after June 3, 2023 to be completed. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-compliance
#| fig-cap: "FRA page limit compliance for post-FRA decarbonization projects. EISs between 151 and 300 pages may still qualify under the extraordinary-complexity provision."
#| out-width: "90%"

knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d5_figures, "05_fra_compliance.png"))
```

# Caveats and Considerations

Several considerations from the fact sheet should remain front-of-mind when translating these findings into policy recommendations.

**Data quality and completeness remain a structural limitation.** 

- NEPATEC 2.0 assembles documents from multiple sources: EIS records are drawn from EPA's governmentwide EIS database and are broadly representative since 2012, but EA and CE data are substantially complete only for DOE and BLM. This means the dataset captures a large share of the federal decarbonization NEPA universe but not all of it — for example, coverage is thin for agencies like the Corps of Engineers or the Forest Service. 

- Better federal metadata standards, document-linkage practices, and centralized submission requirements would improve nearly every downstream permitting analysis. One coveted data point would be project timeline data. In its current form, all timeline data was extracted directly from document text: this is an inefficient, unwieldy, and somewhat inaccurate process. Future iterations of the  NEPATEC database would benefit greatly from including this as metadata, likely requiring NEPA reviewer to provide a summary of key dates within all NEPA documents. 

- Existing efforts such as PermitAI, CEQ's NEPA data standard, and the ePermit Act move in the right direction, but they do not yet solve the broader fragmentation problem — and significant additional investment in federal data infrastructure is still needed.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.column-margin .review-comment}
I added a point about the importance of timeline data as metadata. Is this ok to keep?
:::
:::

**High CE usage is not automatically a normative success — and the present administration's approach warrants particular scrutiny.** 

- Categorical Exclusions are a legitimate and appropriate tool when applied within statutory bounds: they are designed for classes of actions that experience has shown to have no significant individual or cumulative environmental effects. However, their integrity depends on good-faith implementation and the current administration has applied existing CEs to project types they were not designed to cover. This raises concerns about the accuracy of such applied categorical exclusions and artificially compresses review timelines. Unfortuntely, these practices are not directly observable in NEPATEC — the dataset captures the formal record, not the quality of the underlying analysis. A count of CEs is not the same as an asessment of the quality of a CE determination.

**Faster timelines are not the only policy goal, and speed can come at the cost of quality and legal durability.** 

- Review quality, agency learning, and public legitimacy matter alongside speed. DOI's recent production of EISs in as little as two weeks is a salient example: a document of that scope produced on that timeline raises serious questions about whether meaningful analysis took place, regardless of what the formal record shows. Rushing NEPA reviews may trade short-term permitting speed for downstream litigation risk and larger-than-expected environmental impact — the opposite of what well-designed reform should produce.

**Some of the most important questions remain outside this Phase 1 scope.** 

- In particular, the present work does not directly test whether NEPA was the actual cause of project delay, what were the main triggers of NEPA review, nor does it comprehensively analyze when agencies may have relied on CEs too aggressively.
